_meta.purpose: Follow-on research pass on data/research/orderbook-mechanisms.json (captured 2026-08-21). Finds evidence NOT already in that file: (1) developments since 2026-08-21 on the same 23 items, (2) a genuinely microreactor-scale (not SMR-scale) multi-buyer angle, (3) new precedent classes, (4) more insurance-market depth. Does not re-research anything already in orderbook-mechanisms.json.
empty_results: No public evidence found that Equinix's 20-unit Radiant Kaleidos preorder has grown beyond 20 units or added co-buyers as of Sept 2026 — an April-2026-dated source (jaredwatkins.com/smrintel roundup, snippet-only, not independently verified) still describes it as Equinix's single largest single microreactor commitment.

No successor to UAMPS's collapsed Carbon Free Power Project (a new public-power-consortium subscription-model nuclear project) was found; searches for 'UAMPS new nuclear subscription project 2026' return only retrospectives on the 2023 termination.

EFI Foundation's Cost Stabilization Facility / Model Term Sheet (Jan 2025) has not been adopted by any named real project as of this research — it remains a published proposal plus a generic 'Model Term Sheet' template.

No second Marsh (or other broker) commercial-insurance placement for an advanced-reactor construction project (Oklo, Kairos, X-energy, etc.) beyond the March 2026 TerraPower Kemmerer placement already in orderbook-mechanisms.json was found.
No Lloyd's syndicate or reinsurer publication specifically pricing FOAK microreactor (as opposed to SMR/large-reactor) construction risk was found.

Searches for LNG offtake consortiums and desalination-plant risk pools surfaced only conventional single-project, non-recourse project-finance structures (e.g. Ichthys LNG, Aquasure Victorian Desalination) — not a multi-buyer demand-pooling or risk-pooling mechanism structurally distinct from what orderbook-mechanisms.json already documents via NYSERDA and CVOW; not included as a new precedent because it would be a weak analogy forced to fit.

nuclear_aggregation.name: Army Janus Program — five microreactor vendors, $2.2B, NASA-COTS-modeled milestone contracting
nuclear_aggregation.category: microreactor demand aggregation / DOD portfolio procurement (NEW — not in base file)
nuclear_aggregation.mechanism: On Aug 26, 2026 the Army (with the Defense Innovation Unit) selected five companies to design, build, own, and operate microreactors at five installations under Other Transaction Authority agreements: Antares Nuclear (Fort Bragg, NC), BWXT Advanced Technologies (Fort Campbell, KY), General Atomics Electromagnetic Systems (Fort Hood, TX), Radiant Industries (Fort Benning, GA), and Westinghouse Government Services (Fort Drum, NY). The contracting model is fixed-price and milestone-based — 'a lot of these milestones are based on hardware milestones' — explicitly modeled on NASA's Commercial Orbital Transportation Services (COTS) program, the mechanism that helped enable SpaceX. Companies own and operate the reactors commercially; the Army pays only on verified milestone completion and retains regulatory oversight via a newly established Army Reactor Regulatory Office.
nuclear_aggregation.outcome: Up to $2.2B mobilized across FY2027-2031 for the five-year effort, with a mandate (Executive Order 14299) for at least one Army-regulated reactor operating by Sept 30, 2028. The Army states it anticipates more than 20 microreactors eventually, with additional Army and other-service sites still to be named. Radiant disclosed the largest single tranche: up to $750M to deploy 15 factory-built 1-MWe Kaleidos units by 2030, beginning with a three-unit installation at Fort Benning.
nuclear_aggregation.early_vs_late: Not a single-design orderbook with an early/late price schedule — the opposite structural choice from Equinix's 20-unit single-design preorder. DOD deliberately diversified its first tranche across five COMPETING microreactor designs at five different bases rather than aggregating buyer demand behind one standardized design, functioning as a portfolio hedge rather than a learning-curve-pooling mechanism.
nuclear_aggregation.relevance: This is the microreactor-specific, multi-installation government program the base file's 'nuclear_aggregation' section lacked entirely — it did not mention Janus. It directly answers the research brief's 'DOD microreactor bulk procurement' question, but the answer is nuanced: DOD is NOT pooling multiple bases behind one design (the buyers'-club pattern DOE/EFI describe for SMRs); it is running five parallel single-vendor deals and stating explicitly that success means those vendors going on to sell 'to other buyers beyond just the military' — i.e., DOD is using itself as a beachhead/bridge customer to seed multiple manufacturers toward eventual commercial-scale orderbooks, not building one itself.

nuclear_aggregation.name: Radiant Industries — $750M Janus Program award for 15 additional Kaleidos microreactors
nuclear_aggregation.category: microreactor demand aggregation / second independent multi-unit commitment for one design
nuclear_aggregation.mechanism: Within the Janus Program, Radiant separately disclosed up to $750M to develop and deploy 15 factory-built 1-MWe Kaleidos microreactors by 2030, beginning with a three-unit installation at Fort Benning, Georgia — funded on the same milestone/OTA structure as the rest of Janus, described as 'one of the largest contracts ever issued by DIU' and the largest single award within the Janus Program.
nuclear_aggregation.outcome: Announced Aug 26, 2026. Combined with the Equinix preorder already in the base file (20 units, real deposits, Aug 2025), Radiant now has two independently-negotiated multi-unit Kaleidos commitments from two structurally different buyer types (a commercial data-center operator and the U.S. Army) totaling 35 disclosed units, without those two buyers coordinating with each other or sharing a single orderbook vehicle.
nuclear_aggregation.early_vs_late: Not disclosed for either commitment; no evidence the Army and Equinix per-unit pricing are linked, tiered, or averaged across the combined 35-unit base.
nuclear_aggregation.relevance: Directly extends the base file's most-relevant existing precedent (Equinix–Radiant, item 4) rather than duplicating it: Radiant is now the first microreactor vendor with two separate, uncoordinated multi-unit buyer commitments for the same standardized design — the closest real-world approximation yet of the volume a shared orderbook is meant to produce, even though it emerged from two independent deals rather than a formal buyers'-club vehicle.

precedents.name: Illinois Clean and Reliable Grid Affordability Act (CRGA) — state-mandated 3 GW battery storage bulk procurement, financed on the nuclear-ZEC chassis
precedents.category: state-level bulk procurement / ratepayer-financed demand aggregation (NEW precedent class — not in base file)
precedents.mechanism: Signed into law by Gov. Pritzker (CRGA, SB 25), directs the Illinois Power Agency to competitively procure 3 GW of grid-scale battery storage in tranches through 2027-2028 (first 1 GW solicitation's bidding period closed Aug 2026), targeting commercial operation by end of 2030. Developers are paid a guaranteed long-term (e.g. 20-year) credit, funded by 'a new charge on customer utility bills' — explicitly described as 'similar to the one used to keep the state's nuclear plants operating,' i.e. the same financing chassis as Illinois's existing nuclear zero-emission-credit (ZEC) program.
precedents.outcome: Projected cost ~$9.7B over 20 years against projected consumer savings of ~$13.4B from suppressed PJM/MISO capacity-market prices — a net $3.7B ratepayer benefit over two decades, per program modeling. Utilities are also required to develop virtual power plant (VPP) programs enrolling customer-owned batteries and EV chargers.
precedents.early_vs_late: Not an orderbook with a per-unit price schedule — a state-mandated, competitively-solicited capacity target with a uniform ratepayer-funded credit mechanism, structurally closer to CVOW/NYSERDA (already in base file) than to a manufacturer orderbook.
precedents.relevance: The new precedent class the research brief asked for: a live (2026), state-level, ratepayer-financed BULK PROCUREMENT program for a non-nuclear technology (batteries) that explicitly reuses the SAME financing mechanism (a dedicated utility-bill surcharge) the state already uses to keep its existing nuclear fleet running via ZECs. This is a directly transferable template for how a state could fund its share of a microreactor demand-aggregation vehicle without inventing a new financing chassis — piggyback on an existing nuclear-support surcharge structure rather than building a bespoke SPV from scratch.

precedents.name: NASA COTS-modeled milestone financing (via Army Janus Program) — a fifth distinct 'who bears early-stage risk' model
precedents.category: government demand-catalyst / milestone-based at-risk financing precedent (NEW angle on an existing DOD program)
precedents.mechanism: The Janus Program's fixed-price, milestone-based Other Transaction Authority structure — company retains ownership/equity upside and is paid only when it hits verified hardware or regulatory milestones — is explicitly modeled on NASA's Commercial Orbital Transportation Services program, credited with enabling SpaceX's rise. Applied to microreactors: the government acts as a concentrated first bridge-customer across MULTIPLE competing vendors simultaneously, rather than subsidizing one company's R&D (ARDP) or buying output from an established supplier (OWS-style APA).
precedents.outcome: Five vendors under contract as of Aug 2026; too early for outcome data (nearest historical analog, COTS, took roughly a decade to produce a fully commercial launch provider in SpaceX).
precedents.early_vs_late: Every one of the five initial vendors is treated identically at program launch — no tiered first-mover bonus within Janus itself; the 'early mover' advantage instead accrues to whichever of the five reaches commercial-scale 'Nth-of-a-kind' production first and can then sell to buyers beyond the military.
precedents.relevance: Distinct from every 'who pays whom' model already catalogued in the base file's design_notes (buyer-pool average pricing, DOE first-mover-richest subsidy, manufacturer-eats-early-loss, GAVI flat subsidy, Frontier pay-more-early-for-signal): this is a sixth pattern — government-as-parallel-beachhead-customer across several competing designs at once, deliberately not picking a winner, so as to seed multiple future orderbooks rather than build one itself.

risk_pooling.name: NEIL 2023 Audited Financial Statements — Builders' Risk program and retrospective-premium mechanics (primary-source depth)
risk_pooling.category: nuclear mutual insurance — primary-source financial detail (extends base-file NEIL entry, not a duplicate)
risk_pooling.mechanism: NEIL's own Deloitte-audited 2023 consolidated financial statements (filed with member policyholders) confirm and detail the Builders' Risk program the base file already cites: 'The Builders' Risk program provides property insurance coverage of up to $2.75 billion with a sublimit for delay in start-up, natural hazards, and other perils. Policy periods vary as a result of the complexity and uniqueness of each project,' with 'Coverage for Builders' Risk programs consist[ing] of both facultative and treaty reinsurance participation at various attachment points, with or without the nuclear exposure.' Separately, NEIL's real cost-scaling lever across its Member Nuclear book is a RETROSPECTIVE PREMIUM ADJUSTMENT: the Board may call on Members for proportionate additional premium after the fact to cover losses, capped 'equal to ten times the annualized policy premiums' per Member, with total fleet-wide exposure disclosed as a hard cap: 'The maximum potential retrospective premiums, which could be demanded by the Company as of December 31, from the Members is $2 billion in each of 2023 and 2022.'
risk_pooling.outcome: As of Dec 31, 2023: total assets $5.19B, total policyholders' surplus $4.05B, net premiums earned $288.2M (of which $200.8M direct Member Nuclear), and a $300M distribution declared back to Members reflecting a strong claims year. Non-investment-grade Members must post additional security (letter of credit, deposit premium, financial guarantee, or retrospective-premium insurance) for their contingent retrospective obligation.
risk_pooling.early_vs_late: Not disclosed as a per-unit or per-fleet-size rate card — NEIL does not publish a schedule of how Builders' Risk premiums scale with the number of insured units at signing. The actual risk-sharing lever that scales with loss severity is the RETROSPECTIVE call (up to 10x annualized premium per Member, $2B fleet-wide cap), which is a mutual after-the-fact assessment mechanism, not a declining unit-price curve.
risk_pooling.relevance: Directly responds to the research brief's request for NEIL/ANI product-term depth (deductibles, limits, how coverage scales) using NEIL's own audited financials rather than secondary summaries. The key finding for microreactor design purposes: NEIL's actual scaling mechanism for tail risk is a MUTUAL RETROSPECTIVE ASSESSMENT (all Members share in a call, capped per-Member at 10x their own premium) rather than a per-additional-unit discount — structurally the same 'flat pooled assessment, not declining unit price' logic the base file's design_notes already identified in Price-Anderson, just confirmed here with NEIL's own real numbers.

sources.label: NEIL — Consolidated Financial Statements as of and for the Years Ended December 31, 2023 and 2022 (Deloitte & Touche LLP audit)
sources.quote: The Builders' Risk program provides property insurance coverage of up to $2.75 billion with a sublimit for delay in start-up, natural hazards, and other perils.

design_notes: The DOD Janus Program is the microreactor-specific multi-buyer/multi-base program the base file's nuclear_aggregation section was missing entirely — but it answers the research brief's question in an unexpected direction. Rather than pooling multiple bases' demand behind ONE standardized microreactor design (the buyers'-club pattern EFI/DOE describe for SMRs, and the pattern this research was asked to look for), DOD deliberately diversified its first tranche across FIVE competing designs at five different bases. The Army's own stated success metric — helping 'multiple nuclear companies' develop reactors 'which they can sell to other buyers beyond just the military' — confirms this is a government-as-parallel-beachhead-customer strategy, seeding several future manufacturer orderbooks at once rather than aggregating demand into a single one. A microreactor orderbook design should treat Janus as evidence that DIVERSIFICATION and AGGREGATION are two different, currently-coexisting government/buyer strategies for the same underlying problem (nobody wants to be the lone buyer of an unproven design), not assume DOD chose the aggregation path.

Radiant's Kaleidos is now the closest real-world approximation of the volume a shared orderbook is meant to produce (35 disclosed units across two buyer types: Equinix's 20-unit commercial preorder and the Army's 15-unit Janus award) — but it arrived by ACCIDENT of two independent buyers separately picking the same vendor, not by a formal buyers'-club or SPV vehicle coordinating them. Equinix and the Army do not appear to share pricing, contingency funding, or risk-pool structure with each other. This is a live natural experiment: a genuine shared-orderbook vehicle sitting on top of Radiant's existing 35-unit base (rather than starting from zero) would need far less new demand to reach DOE's cited 30-50-unit microreactor liftoff threshold than the base file's design_notes assumed — worth flagging as the most efficient near-term path to a real microreactor orderbook.

Janus's NASA-COTS-modeled, fixed-price, milestone-based Other Transaction Authority structure is a genuinely new entry in the base file's 'who bears early risk, and how' taxonomy (design_note 2 in orderbook-mechanisms.json, which already catalogues four patterns: buyer-pool flat-average pricing, DOE-style front-loaded first-mover subsidy, manufacturer-eats-early-loss aircraft pricing, and GAVI/Frontier third-party subsidy models). Janus adds a fifth/sixth: government pays ONLY on verified milestone completion (not up front, not as a lump subsidy) and spreads that milestone-financing model across several competing vendors in parallel rather than picking one — functionally converting the government into a distributed beachhead market rather than a single deep-pocketed backstop. A microreactor risk-pool design should treat this as a candidate mechanism for the FOAK-derisking layer specifically, distinct from the cost-overrun-backstop layer EFI/ARC Act address.

A live, non-nuclear state-level precedent for 'reuse the existing nuclear ratepayer-surcharge chassis to fund a NEW bulk-procurement program' now exists: Illinois's Clean and Reliable Grid Affordability Act funds its 3 GW battery-storage mandate through 'a new charge on customer utility bills similar to the one used to keep the state's nuclear plants operating' (i.e., the same mechanism as the state's existing nuclear ZEC program). This is directly relevant to microreactor design because it shows a state doesn't need to invent new ratepayer-financing law to back a bulk-procurement/demand-aggregation vehicle for a new technology — it can extend an existing nuclear-support surcharge structure, which lowers the political and legislative lift for any state considering backing a microreactor buyers' pool.

Every item checked for recency (UAMPS successor project, Equinix-Radiant expansion, EFI CSF real-world adoption, a second Marsh advanced-reactor placement, Lloyd's-specific microreactor pricing) came back empty as of Sept 2026 — none of the base file's proposal-stage mechanisms (EFI's CSF, NIA's deductible/copayment structure) has yet been adopted by a real project, and the one enacted-but-unfunded legislative vehicle (ARC Act) is still sitting in committee seven months after introduction with no confirmed vehicle for passage. The overall picture seven months on from the base file's 2026-08-21 capture is that PROPOSALS have not converted to ADOPTIONS, but the one genuinely new operational program (Janus) emerged from a completely different institutional path (defense acquisition reform, not energy-project-finance policy) than any of the proposals the base file catalogued — worth noting that the mechanism that actually shipped came from the acquisition-reform literature (COTS), not the nuclear-project-finance literature (EFI/NIA/DOE Liftoff).
